1.word_for_word: ṣaḍ-viṃśe — in the twenty-sixth chapter; vismitān gopān — the astonished cowherds; kṛṣṇasya adbhuta-karmabhiḥ — because of Kṛṣṇa's wondrous deeds; nandaḥ garga-uktim āśrāvya — Nanda, by recounting Garga's words; tad-aiśvaryam avarṇayat — described Kṛṣṇa's majesty; samabhyetya nandam — having approached Nanda; abhigamya — coming before him
1.translation: In the twenty-sixth chapter, when the cowherds were astonished by Kṛṣṇa's extraordinary deeds, Nanda recounted the words of Garga and thereby described Kṛṣṇa's divine greatness. ‘Having assembled’ means that they approached Nanda.

2.word_for_word: yad ūcuḥ tad āha — he now states what they said; bālakasya iti — beginning with ‘of this boy’; yad yasmāt adbhutāni karmāṇi — because his deeds are astonishing; tasmāt grāmyeṣu gopāleṣu katham janma arhati — how can one like him have been born among ordinary village cowherds; ātma-jugupsitam — unsuitable to his own nature; ātma-anarham — unworthy of him
2.translation: Śrīdhara now gives the substance of the cowherds' words. Because this boy's deeds are so astonishing, how could such a person properly have taken birth among ordinary village cowherds? Such a birth appears incongruous with his own nature.

3.word_for_word: adbhutāni karmāṇi āhuḥ — they enumerate the wondrous deeds; yaḥ sapta-hāyanaḥ iti — beginning ‘he who is seven years old’; katham bibhrat sthitaḥ — how did he remain holding it; puṣkaram padmam — a lotus; gaja-rāṭ mahā-gajaḥ iva — like a mighty elephant holding a lotus
3.translation: They begin enumerating Kṛṣṇa's wonders: ‘He is only seven years old—how did he stand holding Govardhana?’ Śrīdhara compares the effortless pose to a great elephant holding a lotus.

4.word_for_word: mahā-ojasaḥ mahā-balāyāḥ tanoḥ — of a body endowed with enormous power; vayaḥ āyuḥ yauvanam vā — age, life-span or youth; kālena yathā pīyate — as time consumes these; tadvat — in that same way; katham iti anuvartate — the question ‘how?’ continues
4.translation: The phrase concerns the immense vigor of a powerful body. Just as time consumes age, life and youth, so the wording evokes overwhelming power; the interrogative ‘how could he do this?’ continues through these examples.

5.word_for_word: anasaḥ adhaḥ śayānasya — while lying beneath the cart; māsyasya māsāḥ trayaḥ paricchedakāḥ yasya — when only three months old; udag ūrdhvam caraṇau hinvataḥ — moving his feet upward; prapadena pāda-agreṇa — with the tip of his foot; hatam viparyastam anaḥ — the cart struck and overturned; katham apatat — how did it fall
5.translation: When Kṛṣṇa was lying beneath the cart at only three months of age, he merely moved his feet upward and struck it with the tip of his foot. How, they ask, could that cart have been overturned and made to fall?

6.word_for_word: yaḥ kṛṣṇaḥ daityena hriyamāṇaḥ san — Kṛṣṇa, while being carried away by the demon; tam tṛṇāvartam daityam — that demon Tṛṇāvarta; katham ahan — how did he kill him
6.translation: How did Kṛṣṇa, while being carried away by the demon Tṛṇāvarta, nevertheless kill that very demon?

7.word_for_word: haiyaṅgava-stainye — in stealing fresh butter; nava-nīta-caurye — in the theft of butter; bāhubhyām gacchan — moving with the arms; riṅgan — crawling
7.translation: ‘Stealing haiyaṅgava’ means stealing fresh butter. At that age he moved upon his arms—that is, he crawled.

8.word_for_word: mukhataḥ hantum kāmaḥ yasya tam — the one who wished to kill him with his beak/mouth; baka-veṣam arim — the enemy in the form of the crane Baka; bāhubhyām mukhataḥ katham apāṭayat — how did he tear the beak apart with his two arms
8.translation: How did he seize the enemy disguised as the crane Baka, who intended to kill him with his mouth, and tear that beak apart with his two hands? The same astonished question carries through the following cited deeds.

12.word_for_word: āśī-viṣatamaḥ — possessing the most terrible venom; ati-krūra-viṣaḥ — of exceedingly fierce poison; ahi-indraḥ — king of serpents; tam — that Kāliya
12.translation: The serpent-king Kāliya is described as possessing the most dreadful and fiercely lethal venom.

13.word_for_word: autpattikaḥ — innate, arising from birth; svābhāvikaḥ — natural; katham — how is this possible; kim sarveṣām ātmā ayam syāt — could this boy perhaps be the very Self of all beings; iti śaṅkā — such is their emerging suspicion
13.translation: ‘Innate’ means natural from birth. Their astonishment now rises into a deeper suspicion: ‘Could this boy perhaps be the very Self of all beings?’

14.word_for_word: uktam api — though it has already been said; ati-vismayena — because of extreme astonishment; abhinayena vadanti — they repeat it dramatically; kva sapta-hāyana iti — ‘where is a seven-year-old boy, and where is such a feat?’
14.translation: Although the point has already been made, their amazement is so great that they repeat it emphatically: ‘A seven-year-old boy—how can this possibly be reconciled with such a feat?’

15.word_for_word: prāk śrutam eva garga-ācārya-vākyam — the words of Garga that Nanda had heard earlier; tat-carita-pariśīlanena — through reflecting upon Kṛṣṇa's deeds; nivṛtta-asambhāvanasya nandasya — for Nanda, whose former doubt about their possibility had now been removed; kṛṣṇa-tattva-avabodhakam jātam — those words now became a means of understanding Kṛṣṇa's true nature; sa idānīm tena eva vākyena gopān upadiśati — he now instructs the cowherds with those same words; śrūyatām iti — ‘listen’
15.translation: Nanda had heard Garga's words long before, but by repeatedly contemplating Kṛṣṇa's deeds his former inability to conceive their full meaning disappeared. Those words now became for him a means of understanding Kṛṣṇa's true nature, and he teaches the cowherds by repeating them: ‘Listen.’

22.word_for_word: tasmāt tasya karmasu vismayaḥ na asti — therefore there is no reason for astonishment at his deeds; iti nandasya uktiḥ — this is Nanda's conclusion
22.translation: Nanda's conclusion is: ‘Therefore there is really no cause for astonishment at Kṛṣṇa's deeds.’

23.word_for_word: iti addhā sākṣāt mām prati samādiśya — having thus directly instructed me; garge sva-gṛham gate sati — when Garga had returned home; tadānīm tathā manyamānaḥ api — although even then I understood his words in that way; idānīm kṛṣṇam nārāyaṇasya aṃśam manye — now I regard Kṛṣṇa as an aṃśa/manifestation of Nārāyaṇa; atra hetuḥ — the reason is; akliṣṭa-kāriṇam — one who performs impossible acts without difficulty
23.translation: Nanda says: ‘Garga directly gave me this instruction and then returned home. Even then I accepted what he said, but now I understand Kṛṣṇa to be a manifestation of Nārāyaṇa.’ The reason is the expression ‘performer without strain’: Kṛṣṇa accomplishes such extraordinary acts without the least difficulty.

25.word_for_word: govardhana-uddharaṇam sa-parikaram anusmaran — recalling the lifting of Govardhana together with all its circumstances; prakaṭita-aiśvaryasya śrī-kṛṣṇasya prītim prārthayate — he prays for the favor of Śrī Kṛṣṇa whose majesty was manifested; yajña-viplavena yā ruṭ tayā deve indre varṣati sati — when Indra, enraged by the disruption of his sacrifice, poured rain; vajra-aśma-parṣa-anilaiḥ — with thunderbolts, hail and violent winds; sīdat-pāla-paśu-striyam — where cowherd men, animals and women were suffering; ātma-śaraṇam goṣṭham dṛṣṭvā — seeing the cowherd settlement that had him alone as refuge; anukampī — compassionate; utsmayan hasan — smiling; prauḍhim āviṣkurvan — displaying his sovereign power; śailam utpāṭya — uprooting/lifting the mountain; abalaḥ bālaḥ — though appearing a powerless child; līlā-artham ucchilīndhram yathā — playfully, like a mushroom or umbrella; ekena kareṇa bibhrat — holding it with one hand; goṣṭham apāt — protected the settlement; mahendra-mada-bhit — breaker of mighty Indra's pride; gavām indraḥ — the true Indra/lord of the cows; saḥ śrī-kṛṣṇaḥ naḥ prīyāt — may that Śrī Kṛṣṇa be pleased with us
25.translation: Recalling the lifting of Govardhana in all its detail, Nanda prays for the favor of Śrī Kṛṣṇa whose divine majesty had been openly displayed. Indra, enraged by the interruption of his sacrifice, poured down thunderbolts, hail and violent winds. Seeing the cowherd community—men, women and animals—suffering and having no refuge but himself, Kṛṣṇa compassionately smiled, displayed his sovereign power, lifted the mountain, and, though outwardly only a child, held it effortlessly in one hand like a great umbrella or mushroom and protected all of Vraja. Thus he broke mighty Indra's pride and showed himself to be the true lord of the cows. May that Śrī Kṛṣṇa be pleased with us. The final numerical verse in the electronic text is a scribal/editorial colophon-like addition and is not part of the running explanation.
